# Devadhammajātaka (Ja 6)

**ID:** Ja 6
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Devadhammajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Godlike
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja6
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Devadhammajātaka* (Ja 6) is the sixth story in the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection [von Glasenapp 1966; Schönberger 2012]. According to its narrative frame, the story was delivered by the Buddha while residing at Jetavana concerning a wealthy monk [SuttaCentral]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was born as Prince Mahiṃsāsa [von Glasenapp 1966; DeCaroli 1999]. Following the court intrigue of his stepmother, he went into voluntary forest exile with his brother, where they were joined by their stepbrother Prince Moon [DeCaroli 1999]. There they came upon an enchanted pool guarded by a water demon, variously designated as a *yakkha*, *rakkhasa*, or *dakarakkha* [von Glasenapp 1966; DeCaroli 1999; Schönberger 2012]. Under an injunction granted by King Vessavaṇa, the creature was authorized to capture and devour any person who entered the pond without knowing what constitutes the divine (*devadhamma*) [von Glasenapp 1966; Schönberger 2012].

After his brothers are captured for their ignorance, the Bodhisatta confronts the demon and secures their release by providing the correct definition of divine quality (*devadhamma*), articulated in verse as the internal moral constraints of moral shame (*hiri*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) [von Glasenapp 1966; Anandajoti 2010; Granoff and Shinohara 2012]. Tamed and instructed by the Bodhisatta, the spirit converts to the Dhamma, renounces violence, and receives protection and support [Encyclopedia of Buddhism 2004; DeCaroli 1999]. Later sub-commentarial tradition analyzes the psychological dynamics of this verse, emphasizing social censure and public conscience in relation to *ottappa* [Granoff and Shinohara 2012].

Neither SuttaCentral nor the automated textual analysis of DharmaNexus records any direct Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language parallels in Chinese, Sanskrit, or Tibetan for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja6 — Supplied metadata, English title 'Godlike', opening verse line, and setting at Jetavana.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database query for ja6 — Confirmed lack of automated Pali-internal and cross-language parallels.
- [von Glasenapp 1966] Helmuth von Glasenapp, Buddhism - A Non-Theistic Religion (1966) — Detailed the incarnation of the Bodhisatta as Prince Mahiṃsāsa, Vessavaṇa's decree, and the nature of devadhamma.
- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Anandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses: 551 verses from the Canon (2010) — Provided the English rendering 'True Godliness' and summarized the Bodhisatta's release of his brothers.
- [Encyclopedia of Buddhism 2004] Robert E. Buswell Jr. (ed.), Encyclopedia of Buddhism (2004) — Described the conversion of the vicious yakkha into an active, positive force.
- [DeCaroli 1999] Robert Daniel DeCaroli, Haunting the Buddha: Influence of Indian Spirit Religions on Formation of Buddhism (1999) — Outlined the exile narrative involving Prince Moon, the terminology for the spirit, and the spirit's pacification and support.
- [Schönberger 2012] Sarah-Allegra Schönberger, Kriegsglück und Reichtum: Zur ikonographischen Transformation Bishamon-tens. Indien – Japan (2012) — Cited the text reference (Jātaka 1.6) and Vessavaṇa's permission to the water spirit.
- [Granoff and Shinohara 2012] Phyllis Granoff and Koichi Shinohara (eds.), Sins and Sinners: Perspectives from Asian Religions (2012) — Explained the verse's teaching on hiri and ottappa and the sub-commentary's treatment of fear of censure.
